newsitem.title: JAPAN: WEEK AHEAD-Tokyo stocks to drift, wait for 'tankan'.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Tokyo stocks to drift, wait for 'tankan'.

text.p: Tokyo stocks are likely to drift in the coming week as investors sit back and wait for reassurance that currency market turmoil has stopped and for the Bank of Japan's "tankan" survey of corporate sentiment.
Brokers said the Nikkei average was having trouble keeping its gains after setting a new closing high of 20.681.07 for calendar 1997 on June 16.
But there were no strong reasons to sell, and the Nikkei average was likely to continue to trade within a very narrow range, they added.
"There are potential buyers such as pension funds, but they will probably opt to wait for the tankan before buying," said Katsumichi Shimizu, general manager at Yamaichi Securities.
"The downside should be fairly firm near 20,000, but gains will probably be capped by profit-taking."

The tankan survey of corporate sentiment, which could provide clues on how the Japanese economy is performing after the consumption tax was raised by two percentage points in April, will be released on June 25.
On technical factors, market sources said that the upside was seen at the June 13 intra-day high of 20,815 while near-term support was seen near the 25-day moving average, which is around 20,300.

Brokers said that trade was likely to focus more on laggards, smaller shares and over-the-counter stocks rather than blue-chips and many major issues that have risen considerably and are more than ready for a breather.

"Car maker shares, which led the recent blue-chip rally, are falling further and further into a correction phase, and short-covering of bank and construction issues is almost complete," a broker at a "Big Four" brokerage said.

However, some brokers added that if the yen were to stabilise near 115 to the dollar, which is seen as the ideal level for exporters, pension funds could be coaxed into buying global issues once again.

"Shares such as Sony Corp are showing faint signs of reviving after correcting," said Noboru Yorita, general manager at Tachibana Securities. "If the yen calms down, pension funds could spend the remainder of their allocations on such issues."

Brokers added that interest in information technology-related firms, which sent shares such as Fujitsu Ltd and NTT Data Corp to new highs for calendar 1997 in the past week, was likely to continue in coming sessions.
One broker said concerns over the "millenium bug" will create an immense amount of business for information technology firms.

The "millenium bug" centres on fears that at the turn of the century, many computers will show "00" for the year and interpret it as 1900, potentially causing havoc in computer systems. Companies are now racing to reprogamme old software.
He said financial institutions must also invest in computer software due to demands stemming from Japanese financial reforms.
"The share prices in the sector are undervalued," he said.
On Friday, the Nikkei 225 fell 122.31 points or 0.60 percent to 20,385.54, shedding about 140 points from the previous Friday. During the week it hit a high of 20,681.07 and a low of 20.356.54.
